Give a sixteen-year-old a random date, and he can tell you what he did that day.
On a random-dates quiz he got eighty-three percent right. The comparison group averaged twenty-nine.
Researchers in Poland call him KCL.
But the strange part isn't the dates. It's what his mind does when nobody asks.
At random moments they asked what he was thinking. Thirteen times out of fifteen, it was a memory from his own life. For most people, it's about four in ten.
His mind wanders no more often than anyone's. It just wanders backward.
A song, a smell, a photograph, and the past arrives uninvited.
So the researchers suggest it isn't a bigger memory. It's a lower threshold, a door that opens at the faintest cue.
It's one case, so nobody knows how common this is. Latoon. Voyaging the unseen. Follow for more.
